facts.text: The appellants claimed to be the landlords of the premises.
facts.speaker: LANDLORD
facts.stage: High Court factual recital reproduced in appeal record
unknown: whether the claimed landlord status is legally established on the allowed record
facts.quote: the appellants are claiming themselves to be the landlords

facts.text: The eviction petition alleged that the premises were let to DTC for Rs.3500 per month.
facts.speaker: LANDLORD
unknown: whether DTC was legally the tenant
facts.quote: the premises were let out to respondent No.2, Delhi Transport Corporation [for short "DTC"], on a monthly rental of Rs.3500/-

facts.text: The eviction petition alleged that DTC sublet or assigned the premises to MCD and parted with possession in MCD's favour.
facts.speaker: LANDLORD
unknown: whether any subletting, assignment, or parting with possession actually occurred
whether any transfer covered the whole or only part of the premises
facts.quote: DTC has sublet/assigned the premises in favour of respondent No.1, Municipal Corporation of Delhi [for short "MCD"] and parted with 3 possession in favour of MCD

facts.text: The eviction petition alleged that the transfer or parting with possession occurred without the appellants' written consent.
facts.speaker: LANDLORD
facts.quote: without the written consent of the appellants

facts.text: MCD claimed that it retained legal possession and that rent was being paid by MCD to DTC.
facts.speaker: THIRD_PARTY
facts.stage: High Court factual recital of MCD position
unknown: legal significance of the claimed retained possession
whether the payment was legally rent
facts.quote: MCD had, however, claimed that the legal possession was retained by MCD; rent was being paid by MCD to DTC.

facts.text: The ARC found it admitted that MCD was in possession of the premises and paid Rs.3500 to DTC by cheque as rent.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: Admittedly it is respondent No.2 (MCD) who is in possession of the premises in question. It is also admitted that respondent No.2 (MCD) pays a sum of Rs.3500/- as rent to respondent No.1 (DTC) by way of cheques.

facts.text: The ARC found that the respondents did not assert that written consent of the petitioners had been obtained.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: It is not the case of the respondent that any written consent of the petitioners was obtained in this regard.

facts.text: The ARC held that DTC had either sublet, assigned, or otherwise parted with possession of the premises to MCD illegally.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: respondent no.1 (DTC) has either sublet, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the tenanted premises illegally to respondent No.2 (MCD)

facts.text: The ARCT found a landlord-tenant relationship and found that exclusive possession had been handed to MCD, a separate legal entity, amounting to subletting.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: there exists relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties and since the exclusive possession of the premises was handed over by the erstwhile tenant to the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, i.e., respondent No.2 which is itself a separate and independent legal entity, it amounts to sub- letting.

facts.text: The High Court found that there was no parting with possession by DTC to MCD and therefore no subletting.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: There was no parting with possession by DTC to MCD, therefore, it was not sub-letting.

facts.text: The High Court found that the Rs.3500 monthly payment by MCD to DTC did not itself show subletting or parting with possession.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: Mere payment of Rs.3500/- per month by MCD to DTC does not show sub-letting or parting with possession.

facts.text: The High Court described GNIT as having been acquired by legislation, the premises going to DTS, DTS being converted to DTU, and DTU being converted into DTC.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: The alleged original tenant GNIT stood acquired by a cite14†Legislative Act and the premises went to DTS. DTS was converted to DTU and DTU was further converted into DTC.

facts.text: The High Court stated that the lower courts had not considered who the tenant was or how MCD became a sub-tenant after the premises were owned by the Union of India and the land's leasehold rights vested in it.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: The Courts below did not even consider the issue as to who was the tenant and how MCD became the sub-tenant of respondent once the premises was owned by Union of India and the leasehold rights of the entire land vested in Union of India.

facts.text: Counsel for the respondents claimed that the appellants had failed to prove any parting with possession without written landlord consent, that MCD retained legal possession all along, and that the Rs.3500 payment was routed through DTC for convenience.
facts.speaker: UNKNOWN
facts.stage: respondents' submissions on Supreme Court appeal
unknown: whether MCD in fact retained legal possession throughout
facts.quote: the appellants have failed to prove that there has been any parting with possession, without the written consent of the landlord. The ARC and ARCT ignored vital documents in concluding that there has been subletting by DTC to MCD. In fact, MCD has retained the legal possession all along.

facts.text: Counsel for the respondents claimed that no landlord-tenant relationship existed between the appellants' predecessor and GNIT.
facts.speaker: UNKNOWN
facts.stage: respondents' submissions on Supreme Court appeal
unknown: legal identity of the relevant original tenant
facts.quote: According to the learned counsel, there was no landlord and tenant relationship between the predecessor of the appellants and GNIT.

issue_needs_context_not_application_targ.text: Who held the relevant landlord, tenant, and legal-possession positions for the premises during the alleged subletting or assignment?
Did DTC sublet, assign, or otherwise part with possession of the whole or any part of the premises to MCD, considering the competing descriptions of possession and the Rs.3500 payment?
Was the alleged subletting, assignment, or parting with possession undertaken without the landlord's written consent?

How does the asserted statutory acquisition and succession from GNIT through DTS and DTU to DTC, together with the asserted continuity of MCD possession, bear on whether there was a legally distinct transfer or parting with possession?

What temporal and procedural predicates relevant to the supplied Delhi provisions are established or left unresolved, including the date of the alleged transfer and any facts concerning lawful sub-tenancy notice or protected sub-tenant status?
